chapters.title: The long tenon and the komisen

narration.text: A post comes down onto a sill. A tongue on its end slides into a hole, and a square pin is driven across, pulling the two tight together.
This is the mortise and tenon: in Japanese, hozo and hozo-ana.
Hozo is the tenon, the tongue. Hozo-ana, literally tenon hole, is the mortise. Dictionaries note an older reading, hoso.

There are many named kinds. A stepped tenon, the jūhozo, or stacked tenon, for example, goes at the top of a post where a wall plate and a beam stack up. This episode looks at the joint where a post meets a sill.
For posts outside the bearing walls, the Flat 35 house specification lists two families of options. A short tenon, held with a metal plate, bracket or staple. Or a long tenon, pinned with a komisen.
At an outside corner, the corner post can take the ōgi-hozo, a fan tenon with a trapezoid section, again with hardware.
How big is a short tenon? The test standard for Japan's certified joint hardware uses one on a hundred-and-five millimeter post and sill: thirty thick, eighty-five wide, fifty deep.

In a bearing wall, Japan's standard detail drawings give a plain short tenon a joint rating of zero: it isn't counted on to stop the post pulling out. That job needs rated hardware, or a pinned long tenon.

The long tenon goes deep into the sill. A hardwood pin, the komisen, is driven sideways through sill and tenon together. Where a tenon passes right through and sticks out, it can instead be pinned through that projecting part: a hanasen.

The holes are made so the pin draws the two members together: the hole through the tenon is bored slightly closer to the shoulder than the hole through the sill. Driving the pin pulls the post down tight onto the sill.

The public-works specification asks for square holes and pins; one lab report notes round pins are now more common. In a bearing wall, the Flat 35 specification puts a pinned long tenon in the same class as an L-shaped metal corner plate.
Cutting the tenon: rip down the cheeks first, then crosscut the shoulder, with the kerf on the waste side of its line. The public-works specification warns: don't saw the crosscuts too deep.
In the skills-test manual's practice piece, a beam's tenon is cut a little loose in thickness and a little tight in width, as we saw in Episode 4.
Chopping the mortise: use a mortise chisel a little narrower than the hole. Start a few millimeters inside the lines, rough it out, then pare back to the lines and check the depth.
The manual adds: strike lightly when the edge runs along the grain, and a little harder when it cuts across it.

Fit it in small steps. In the manual's practice piece, the width goes in with light taps over a block of wood; the thickness, by hand. For posts, the public-works specification asks for a snug fit: driven in, and fully seated.
Next time: where one beam crosses over another.
A short tenon needs hardware to hold. A long tenon can be pinned so it pulls itself tight. And a snug fit, made in small steps, does the rest.
One note: sharp-tool technique, and how to use these tools safely, is best learned from a teacher, at a bench, in person.
